{"id": "96:1/q06", "question": "Why does 'Read' precede 'in your Lord's name'?", "turns_on": "Whether the command is foregrounded or the prepositional phrase belongs to the later repetition.", "positions": [{"id": "96:1/q06/p1", "position": "The verb comes first to emphasize the urgent, initial command to read.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān gives the urgency of the act in the first revealed sūra as reason to put the verb first. BURHAN: Two explanations are offered for placing the verb before “in the name of your Lord”: the act is foremost because this was the first revealed sūrah, or the phrase attaches to the second “recite.”; cites 96:1 BIQAI: The verb is placed before its prepositional phrase for greater impact, especially as this was the first revelation and reading was the urgent command; its object is omitted to indicate that the reading commanded is the Qurʾān, comprehensive of all good. BIQAI-FULL: The active verb is placed before its prepositional phrase because this is more forceful, especially in the first revelation, where the command to read is paramount. ALUSI: Al-Ālūsī prefers attaching “in your Lord’s name” to the adjacent verb; placing the verb first suits this opening surah, where recitation is especially important. ALUSI-FULL: The fronted command suits the importance of reading in the first surah revealed; even if another passage preceded it, the sense is read beginning with God's name, so other openings would not comply, while moving the name first changes the focus."}, {"id": "96:1/q06/p2", "position": "The prepositional phrase can be construed with the second 'Read'.", "reasons": "BURHAN: Two explanations are offered for placing the verb before “in the name of your Lord”: the act is foremost because this was the first revealed sūrah, or the phrase attaches to the second “recite.”; cites 96:1 ALUSI (بعضهم): Another analysis leaves “in God’s name” with its customary attachment, treats recite as initiating the reading, and attaches “your Lord” to the second command. ALUSI (من علق الجار بالثاني): Those attaching the phrase to the second command answer that the first command already establishes recitation itself as required. Against—ALUSI (بعضهم): A very remote analysis attaches “in the name” in the basmala to the first recite and “in your Lord’s name” to the second, making the fronting specify God’s name as the required opening. Against—ALUSI-FULL: Al-Alusi says the clearest interpretation is that the second Read reinforces the first; the proposal to attach the basmala's باسم to the second command to make God's name the exclusive starting point is far-fetched because it normally attaches to the adjacent command."}, {"id": "96:1/q06/p3", "position": "It attaches to the adjacent first command; moving it before the verb would shift the emphasis to God's name.", "reasons": "ALUSI: Al-Ālūsī prefers attaching “in your Lord’s name” to the adjacent verb; placing the verb first suits this opening surah, where recitation is especially important. ALUSI: Fronting the prepositional phrase would instead make opening in God’s name the requested act, while recitation itself would be presupposed rather than commanded. ALUSI-FULL: Al-Alusi says the clearest interpretation is that the second Read reinforces the first; the proposal to attach the basmala's باسم to the second command to make God's name the exclusive starting point is far-fetched because it normally attaches to the adjacent command. ALUSI-FULL: The fronted command suits the importance of reading in the first surah revealed; even if another passage preceded it, the sense is read beginning with God's name, so other openings would not comply, while moving the name first changes the focus."}]}
{"id": "96:1/q07", "question": "Why is 'Read' repeated later in the opening passage?", "turns_on": "Whether repetition reinforces one command or distinguishes purposes of two readings.", "positions": [{"id": "96:1/q07/p1", "position": "The second command reinforces and comforts after the Prophet's hesitation.", "reasons": "BURHAN (الأصمعي): The anonymous poetic lines repeat النوى, separation, and al-Aṣmaʿī jokes that the second version deserved a she-goat, illustrating the effect of repeated wording. BURHAN: Poetic repetition of حديث and the beloved's dwelling shows how repeating a subject can delight the listener. BIQAI-FULL: Repeating “Read” emphasizes the command, comforts the Prophet, and distinguishes the One who brings revelation from the false objects of worship; the Prophet had said he could not read. BURSEVI: Iqra is a command, repeated to reinforce the obligation and introduce a new sentence about the most generous Lord; a permissible pause follows خلق because the Prophet had objected that he could not read. ALUSI-FULL: Al-Alusi says the clearest interpretation is that the second Read reinforces the first; the proposal to attach the basmala's باسم to the second command to make God's name the exclusive starting point is far-fetched because it normally attaches to the adjacent command. IBNASHUR-FULL: The second command to recite repeats the first to give it additional emphasis. BINTSHATI: She prefers the straightforward context: the command to recite is reiterated, and revelation specifies what the Prophet should read in his Lord’s name."}, {"id": "96:1/q07/p2", "position": "The first is personal or general reading; the second is public proclamation.", "reasons": "ALUSI-FULL (الجبائي): Al-Jubbai says the first Read commands personal reading or reading generally, while the second is reading for proclamation; another view connects the latter to prayer, and the Lord's generosity clause could be circumstantial or independent. BINTSHATI (بعض المفسرين): Some exegetes, as al-Razi transmits, say the first اقرأ is for the Prophet himself and the second for proclamation to others."}, {"id": "96:1/q07/p3", "position": "The two commands distinguish reading in prayer from reading outside it.", "reasons": "ALUSI-FULL (الجبائي): Al-Jubbai says the first Read commands personal reading or reading generally, while the second is reading for proclamation; another view connects the latter to prayer, and the Lord's generosity clause could be circumstantial or independent. BINTSHATI (بعض المفسرين): A third reported interpretation says the first recitation is in prayer and the second outside prayer."}, {"id": "96:1/q07/p4", "position": "The first is learning; the second teaching.", "reasons": "BINTSHATI (بعض المفسرين): A second reported interpretation makes the first command to read for learning and the second to teach."}]}
{"id": "96:1/q08", "question": "What does 'in the name of your Lord' direct the reader to do?", "turns_on": "The force of bāʾ: beginning with invocation, direct object, aid, dedication, accompaniment, or permission.", "positions": [{"id": "96:1/q08/p1", "position": "Begin recitation by invoking God's name, often with the basmala.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj supplies an understood 'I began'; al-Māwardī and al-Kashshāf take the phrase as beginning recitation while saying bismillah. Ibn ʿAṭiyya cites 11:41, the command to board in God's name. Al-Qurṭubī parses it as a circumstantial accusative; al-Nasafī likewise says say bismillah and then read. BIQAI: Reading in the Lord's name may mean beginning with the basmala, seeking help from the beneficent Lord, or mentioning His name; on the last reading, the name stands for His sublime attributes. BIQAI: The opening functions like a longer, more reassuring basmala: it alludes to the Greatest Name through the full set of perfect attributes, universal mercy through creation, and particular mercy through honor and teaching that guides to divine approval. BIQAI-FULL: “In the name of your Lord” means beginning with the basmala, seeking the benefactor's aid, or mentioning His name; in the last reading, the name stands for His exalted attributes. ALUSI: The bāʾ is original and marks association; it attaches to iqraʾ or to an omitted circumstantial expression, so the command means begin or open by God's name. ALUSI (قتادة): A reading attributed to Qatāda takes the bāʾ phrase as an omitted circumstantial expression: read while beginning with your Lord's name. ALUSI: On this reading one must begin by saying in God's name; opening with another name would not fulfill the command. ALUSI (قتادة): Qatāda explains the command as beginning in the Lord’s name: say “In God’s name,” then recite; without the basmala, or with an idol’s name, the command would not be fulfilled. ALUSI-FULL (قتادة): According to a reading attributed to Qatada, the command means begin or open with your Lord's name, saying the basmala and then reading; this supports requiring basmala when reading and has been used to argue it belongs to every surah, though al-Alusi notes debate. ALUSI-FULL: Al-Alusi prefers the ba as accompaniment because that avoids implying God's name is an instrument; it may alternatively indicate seeking aid. ELMALILI: The command miraculously gave the unlettered Prophet a book to recite, teach, and dictate without writing himself; beginning with the basmala accords with God's lordship. ELMALILI: The command means to begin reading in the name of the Lord, starting with God's exalted name. ELMALILI: The third command began the Qur'an and simultaneously miraculously made the unreading Prophet able to read, fixed the text to be recited, and taught him to introduce the Creator, as related to 29:48 and 42:52.; cites 29:48, 42:52 IBNASHUR: One analysis begins the recitation with “In God's name”: bi marks assistance and attaches either to an omitted “begin” or to a second “read,” fronted to emphasize God's name; it implies Muhammad uttered the phrase on receiving the revelation. TABATABAI: ‘In the name of your Lord’ attaches to an implied ‘beginning’ or to ‘read’ with the ba of accompaniment; the basmala is part of the surah and God teaches by having the Prophet begin with it. BINTSHATI: The command is to recite in the name of the Creator, the rightful Lor

d rather than the idols the Arabs had fashioned and then worshiped. Rāzī rejects the analysis because it discards the bāʾ without benefit and fails to explain Muhammad's reply. BURHAN: باء also appears with objects in examples such as بأيديكم, بالمودة, باسم ربك, and بأيكم المفتون; المفتون is a passive participle, not a verbal noun.; cites 68:6, 76:6, 22:25, 23:20, 4:43 BIQAI: Reading in the Lord's name may mean beginning with the basmala, seeking help from the beneficent Lord, or mentioning His name; on the last reading, the name stands for His sublime attributes. ALUSI-FULL: Read has an implied object, what is revealed of the Quran; the verb is not intransitive and باسم ربك is not its object with an extra ba, contrary to Abu Ubayda. BIQAI: Reading in the Lord's name may mean beginning with the basmala, seeking help from the beneficent Lord, or mentioning His name; on the last reading, the name stands for His sublime attributes. BIQAI-FULL: “In the name of your Lord” means beginning with the basmala, seeking the benefactor's aid, or mentioning His name; in the last reading, the name stands for His exalted attributes. IBNASHUR: One analysis begins the recitation with “In God's name”: bi marks assistance and attaches either to an omitted “begin” or to a second “read,” fronted to emphasize God's name; it implies Muhammad uttered the phrase on receiving the revelation. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR: Reading can mean in the Creator Lord's name or for the Creator; every reading or activity should begin with, serve, and seek help from God rather than another being. Against—ALUSI: The bāʾ can also mean seeking assistance, but association is preferable because it avoids making God's name an instrument for something else. Against—ALUSI-FULL: Al-Alusi prefers the ba as accompaniment because that avoids implying God's name is an instrument; it may alternatively indicate seeking aid."}, {"id": "96:1/q08/p4", "position": "The bāʾ has the force of ʿalā, 'upon'.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash, reported by Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn, compares 11:41, boarding the ship 'upon' God's name. Al-Qurṭubī gives the same force and supplies the omitted Qurʾān as object."}, {"id": "96:1/q08/p5", "position": "Recite with awareness of God's name and majesty.", "reasons": "ALUSI: The bāʾ is original and marks association; it attaches to iqraʾ or to an omitted circumstantial expression, so the command means begin or open by God's name. ALUSI (قتادة): A reading attributed to Qatāda takes the bāʾ phrase as an omitted circumstantial expression: read while beginning with your Lord's name. ALUSI: The bāʾ can also mean seeking assistance, but association is preferable because it avoids making God's name an instrument for something else. ALUSI-FULL (أبو عبيدة): Abu Ubayda treats the ba as extra and reads the command as Remember your Lord; al-Alusi rejects this, taking the ba as original accompaniment attached to read or an implied circumstantial phrase. TABATABAI: ‘In the name of your Lord’ attaches to an implied ‘beginning’ or to ‘read’ with the ba of accompaniment; the basmala is part of the surah and God teaches by having the Prophet begin with it."}, {"id": "96:1/q08/p6", "position": "Dedicate recitation to God, so it is for His sake.", "reasons": "Rāzī says dedication to God puts the act beyond Satan's interference; naming God before eating prevents Satan sharing it, and a neutral act becomes worship when it aids obedience. {"id": "96:1/q14", "question": "Why is God called 'your Lord' here?", "turns_on": "Whether it foregrounds nurturing, reassurance, unique allegiance, or active lordship.", "positions": [{"id": "96:1/q14/p1", "position": "The title recalls God's nurture and care for Muhammad and reassures him amid fear.", "reasons": "Rāzī argues the frightened Prophet is reassured that the one who began caring for him will complete that care; creation from nonexistence is itself nurturing. Abū Ḥayyān stresses protection and welfare. BIQAI: Rather than the all-encompassing Greatest Name, the verse uses the nurturing Lord's attribute, gathering the other attributes and comforting the Prophet as the first revelation came while he loved solitude in worship at Ḥirāʾ. BIQAI-FULL: The Lord's nurturing attribute, rather than the encompassing divine name, comforts the Prophet and recalls the favors recalled in al-Sharḥ; the command came when he loved retreat for worship in Ḥirāʾ.; cites 94:1-8 BIQAI-FULL: Both names point to the command: the Lord who nurtures deserves thanks, while reading signals the command to worship and implies salvation at the final judgment. ALUSI: Calling God the Prophet's Lord evokes nurturing and gradual development toward fitting perfection; the possessive pronoun signals that revelation brings him to the highest human completion. ALUSI: The description recalls God's first favor to the Prophet and signals God's power to teach him to read in the gentlest way. ALUSI-FULL: Who created recalls God's original favor and ability to teach reading; it may mean the one who creates or the one who created everything, and it rules out idols as true lords because Arabs did not ascribe creation to them. ALUSI-FULL: Calling God Lord and adding the possessive for Muhammad recalls divine nurturing and his gradual attainment of human perfection through recurring revelation. IBNASHUR: Calling God “your Lord” rather than using the proper name Allah evokes care for the one nurtured and, with the possessive pronoun, rejects rivals claimed as lords; the verse grounds Islamic monotheism. BINTSHATI (الفخر الرازي): Al-Razi says Rabbika comforts the Prophet: God has nurtured him from an embryo into a knowing believer, so he should neither fear nor expect abandonment; the command also obliges him to act. BINTSHATI (أبو حيان): Abu Hayyan says Rabbuka comforts Muhammad and identifies his exclusive Lord; the Creator attribute follows because Arabs called idols lords, though idols cannot create."}, {"id": "96:1/q14/p2", "position": "The possessive address marks God's special relation to Muhammad and excludes rival lords.", "reasons": "Rāzī cites 17:1 and 4:80 for reciprocal relation between God and Messenger; Abū Ḥayyān says the possessive address signals intimacy and no other lord.
